title: Best Mixers to Avoid a Hangover: Soda vs Tonic vs Juice vs Diet
excerpt: What's the best mixer for vodka to avoid a hangover? An honest ranking of soda water, tonic, juice, diet mixers, and energy drinks, and what actually matters more than the mixer.
metaDescription: The best mixer for vodka to avoid a hangover, ranked: soda water vs tonic vs juice vs diet soda vs energy drinks, and what matters more than your mixer.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best mixer to avoid a hangover is plain soda water (club soda or seltzer) or, even better, still water on the side. Mixers don't change how much alcohol you drink, and that is still the biggest driver of how you feel the next day. But they do change how fast you drink, how fast the alcohol reaches your blood, and how much sugar and caffeine you take in along the way. Pick a mixer that is low in sugar, free of caffeine, and easy to sip slowly, pair it with a clear spirit like vodka or gin, and you've done most of what a mixer can do for you.

**The quick ranking:** soda water and still water are the safest choices. Fresh citrus, coconut water, and small splashes of juice are fine. Regular soda, tonic, and sugary juices are okay in moderation but make it easy to drink faster. Diet mixers can raise your blood alcohol more than you'd expect. Energy drinks are the one mixer we'd tell you to skip.

> **A note on safety.** This article is general information for adults who drink socially. It is not medical advice. No mixer makes heavy drinking safe, and none of them will prevent a hangover if you drink a lot. If you take regular medication, check with a pharmacist before mixing alcohol with grapefruit juice or caffeinated drinks. If someone is very confused, vomiting repeatedly, breathing slowly, or hard to wake after drinking, call 911 (or your local emergency number). Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not a bad hangover.

## Why Your Mixer Matters at All

It's tempting to think the mixer is just flavor. It isn't quite that simple. A mixer can affect your night and your next morning in four ways.

1. **How fast you drink.** Sweet, cold, fizzy drinks go down easily. When a drink tastes like soda, it's easy to finish it in ten minutes instead of thirty. Drinking speed matters because your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for most adults. Drink faster than that and alcohol piles up in your blood.
2. **How fast the alcohol is absorbed.** Carbonation and the presence or absence of sugar can change how quickly alcohol moves from your stomach into your small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. Faster absorption means a higher peak blood alcohol level from the same drink.
3. **What else you're putting in your body.** Sugar, caffeine, and acids add their own effects. Caffeine can hide how drunk you are. Lots of sugar can leave you feeling worse in the morning, mostly because it encourages more drinking.
4. **Whether you're also getting fluid.** A tall drink with plenty of mixer gives you more fluid per unit of alcohol than a short, strong one. That doesn't cancel alcohol's effect on your kidneys, but it helps a little and slows you down.

Notice what isn't on that list: a mixer can't neutralize alcohol, flush it out faster in any meaningful way, or stop your body from turning it into acetaldehyde, the toxic by-product linked to many hangover symptoms. For the full picture of what causes a hangover and how to cut the risk, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## The Best Mixer for Vodka to Avoid a Hangover

If you drink vodka, you're already off to a decent start. Vodka is one of the "cleanest" spirits, meaning it has very low levels of congeners. Congeners are the extra chemicals produced during fermentation and aging that give darker drinks their flavor and color. A well-known study led by Damaris Rohsenow and published in 2010 had people drink either bourbon or vodka to the same blood alcohol level, and the bourbon drinkers reported worse hangovers on average. Our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes into more detail. And for the drinks that stack sugar, congeners, and strength in one glass, see our list of the [worst cocktails for hangovers](/never-hungover/worst-cocktails-for-hangovers).

The catch is that the low-congener advantage is easy to throw away with the wrong mixer. Here's how the common vodka pairings stack up.

**1. Vodka soda (best).** Vodka with club soda or seltzer and a squeeze of lime has almost no sugar, no caffeine, and nothing else to complicate things. It's not very sweet, so most people sip it more slowly than a cocktail. The one downside is the carbonation, which we cover below. If that's a concern, make it a tall glass with plenty of ice and drink a glass of water alongside it.

**2. Vodka and water, or vodka on the rocks with a water chaser.** This is the cleanest option of all, but most people don't enjoy it. A water chaser after every drink does more good than the mixer itself.

**3. Vodka with fresh citrus.** A splash of fresh lime, lemon, or grapefruit adds flavor without much sugar. A vodka soda with a lot of fresh lime is one of the best-tasting low-sugar drinks you can order.

**4. Vodka cranberry.** A classic, and fine in moderation. Cranberry juice cocktail is usually sweetened, so it's sugarier than it tastes. Asking for half cranberry and half soda cuts the sugar and stretches the drink.

**5. Vodka tonic.** Tonic water tastes bitter, so people assume it's low in sugar. It isn't. Regular tonic has a sugar content close to a regular soda. It's not a bad choice, just not the "light" one it seems.

**6. Vodka with regular soda (cola, lemon-lime).** Sweet and very easy to drink fast. Fine for one, risky for a night.

**7. Vodka with diet soda.** Lower in calories, but there's evidence it raises your blood alcohol more than the sugared version (see below).

**8. Vodka Red Bull or other energy drinks (avoid).** The caffeine makes it harder to tell how drunk you are, which tends to lead to drinking more. More on this later.

For more on why vodka hangovers still happen even with a clean spirit, see our guide to the [vodka hangover](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide).

## Soda Water, Club Soda, and Seltzer

These three get used interchangeably at the bar, and for hangover purposes the differences are small.

- **Seltzer** is plain water with added carbon dioxide.
- **Club soda** is carbonated water with small amounts of added minerals, such as sodium bicarbonate or potassium salts, which give it a slightly salty taste.
- **Sparkling mineral water** (like the brands from natural springs) is naturally or artificially carbonated water that contains whatever minerals came from its source.

The tiny amount of minerals in club soda or mineral water isn't enough to rehydrate you in any real sense, but it doesn't hurt. Any of the three is a great mixer: no sugar, no calories, no caffeine.

### Does carbonation make you drunk faster?

Possibly, for some people. The idea is that bubbles speed up the emptying of your stomach into your small intestine, where alcohol is absorbed quickly. A small UK study published in 2007 (Roberts and Robinson) compared vodka mixed with still water against vodka mixed with carbonated water, and most of the participants absorbed alcohol faster with the fizzy version. Some didn't, and a few absorbed it more slowly, so the effect varies a lot from person to person.

This is also part of why champagne and sparkling wine can feel like they "hit faster."

In practice, this isn't a reason to avoid soda water. A faster rise in blood alcohol matters most when you're drinking quickly. A vodka soda that you sip over 45 minutes with a water on the side is still a better choice than a sugary still cocktail you finish in ten. If you notice that fizzy drinks hit you harder, switch to still water as a mixer, or just slow down.

## Tonic Water: Better or Worse?

Tonic gets its bitter taste from quinine, a compound that was once used to treat malaria. The amount in modern tonic water is small and regulated, and it's not a concern for most people at normal drinking amounts.

The main thing to know about tonic is the sugar. Because the bitterness hides the sweetness, regular tonic tastes less sugary than it is. A gin and tonic or vodka tonic made with a full can of regular tonic carries a similar sugar load to a rum and cola.

Options if you like tonic:

- **Light or slimline tonic** cuts the sugar a lot. (See the next section on diet mixers for the trade-off.)
- **Half tonic, half soda water** keeps the flavor but cuts the sugar roughly in half.
- **A small "splash" of tonic** in a tall soda water works well too.

There's no good evidence that quinine itself makes hangovers better or worse. Tonic is a middle-of-the-pack mixer: not harmful, just not as clean as it looks.

## Juice Mixers: Orange, Cranberry, Pineapple, and Grapefruit

Juice has some real points in its favor. It brings fluid, a little potassium, and some vitamin C. Some people find a juice-based drink sits better on their stomach than straight spirits.

The downsides:

- **Sugar.** Fruit juice is high in natural sugar, and many bar juices (especially "cranberry juice cocktail" and pineapple mixes) have extra sugar added.
- **Easy drinking.** Juice hides the taste of alcohol very well, which is exactly why screwdrivers and punches can sneak up on people.
- **Acid.** Citrus juices are acidic. If you get heartburn or stomach upset when you drink, orange and grapefruit juice may make it worse.

### Does juice help your body clear alcohol?

You'll sometimes hear that the fructose in fruit juice speeds up how fast your liver gets rid of alcohol. Some older studies did look at this, with mixed and modest results. There is no good evidence that drinking juice with alcohol sobers you up faster or prevents a hangover in any way you'd notice. Treat juice as a flavor choice, not a remedy.

### A warning about grapefruit juice

Grapefruit juice interferes with an enzyme (CYP3A4) that your body uses to break down many common medicines, including some statins, blood pressure drugs, and anti-anxiety medicines. That can raise the level of those drugs in your blood. This isn't a problem with alcohol itself, but if you take regular medication, check the label or ask a pharmacist before making grapefruit your go-to mixer.

**Our take on juice:** a splash of fresh juice in a tall soda water is a great compromise. A full glass of sweetened juice with a heavy pour is the version to limit.

## Diet Mixers: The Surprising Trade-Off

Diet soda and diet tonic seem like an obvious upgrade. No sugar, no calories. But there's one catch worth knowing about.

Sugar in your stomach slows down how quickly it empties into your small intestine. When you remove the sugar, the alcohol moves through faster and is absorbed faster. Researchers Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates tested this in a 2013 study in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research*. Participants drank the same amount of vodka mixed with either a regular or a diet soft drink. When they had the diet version, their breath alcohol readings were noticeably higher, and they didn't feel any more drunk. That gap between how drunk you are and how drunk you feel is the risky part, especially if you're thinking of driving.

So which is better for a hangover? It's honestly a trade-off:

- **Diet mixers** save you a lot of sugar and calories but can push your blood alcohol higher per drink.
- **Regular mixers** blunt the alcohol peak a little but add a lot of sugar and are easy to over-drink.

The practical answer is that the mixer type matters less than the pace. If you use diet mixers, treat each drink as slightly stronger than it feels, space them out, and eat beforehand. Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption far more than any mixer does.

## Energy Drinks: The One Mixer to Skip

Vodka Red Bull, Jägerbombs, and similar drinks are popular because the caffeine makes people feel more awake and energetic. That's exactly the problem.

Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol at all. It just hides some of the sleepiness that normally tells you you've had enough. People sometimes call this being "wide-awake drunk." You feel more sober than you are, so you tend to keep drinking, and you may make decisions (like driving) you wouldn't make if you felt as drunk as you really were. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) warns that mixing alcohol with energy drinks is linked to drinking more and to higher rates of risky behavior. In 2010 the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warned makers of pre-mixed caffeinated alcoholic drinks that the added caffeine was an unsafe additive, and those products were reformulated.

For your hangover specifically, energy drinks add a few more problems:

- **Worse sleep.** Caffeine stays in your system for hours. Combined with alcohol, which already breaks up your sleep in the second half of the night, it can leave you waking up exhausted.
- **Lots of sugar** in the regular versions.
- **A racing heart** for some people, since both caffeine and alcohol can raise heart rate.

Our full guide on [energy drinks and alcohol](/never-hungover/energy-drinks-and-alcohol) covers the risks in more detail. If you want caffeine, have a coffee the next morning instead.

## Cola and Other Caffeinated Sodas

Rum and Coke and whiskey Coke are the mild cousins of the energy-drink problem. A can of cola has much less caffeine than a typical energy drink, but it isn't zero, and it's paired with a lot of sugar. One or two won't make much difference. A whole night of them adds up to a fair amount of both caffeine and sugar, which won't help your sleep. Caffeine-free versions exist and are a simple swap if you're sensitive.

## Coconut Water, Electrolyte Drinks, and Other "Healthy" Mixers

Some people use coconut water or electrolyte drinks as mixers on the theory that they'll hydrate you while you drink.

The thinking makes some sense. Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin, which normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you urinate more than you drink. Coconut water contains potassium, and electrolyte drinks contain sodium and other minerals.

The reality is more modest. A mixer can't fully offset the extra urination caused by alcohol, and dehydration is only one part of a hangover. Research suggests hangover severity doesn't line up neatly with how dehydrated people are, which is why drinking water alone rarely fixes a bad one. Our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) walks through this.

That said, coconut water is a perfectly good mixer. It's lower in sugar than most juices and pairs well with rum or vodka. Electrolyte drinks work too, though many sports drinks are sugary. Just don't assume a "healthy" mixer lets you drink more.

## Dark Spirits and Mixers

If you prefer whiskey, rum, or brandy, your mixer choice still matters, but it can't undo the higher congener content of darker spirits. A whiskey with soda water is a better choice than a whiskey with cola, but it will generally still be harder on the morning after than a vodka soda at the same strength, for people who are sensitive to congeners.

If you want the lowest-hangover drink overall, a clear spirit with soda water is the combination to aim for. Our ranking of [the least hangover-prone types of alcohol](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked) compares the options side by side.

## What About Sugar and Hangovers?

It's widely believed that sugary drinks cause worse hangovers. The direct evidence for that is thinner than you'd expect. The biggest effect of sugar is probably indirect: sweet drinks are easy to drink quickly and mask the taste of alcohol, so people end up drinking more in less time. Sugary cocktails also tend to be the ones with several types of alcohol in them, like Long Island iced teas, which pack a lot of alcohol into one glass.

There's also a reasonable case that a big sugar load followed by a night of poor sleep leaves you feeling sluggish, but that's hard to separate from the alcohol itself. Our guide on [sugar and hangovers](/never-hungover/sugar-for-hangover) looks at what the evidence does and doesn't show.

The takeaway is simple: low-sugar mixers make it easier to drink slowly and keep track of what you've had.

## How to Order (or Mix) a Lower-Hangover Drink

Putting it all together, here's what to ask for at the bar or make at home.

- **Vodka soda with fresh lime.** The default low-hangover order.
- **Gin and soda with a splash of tonic.** All the gin and tonic flavor with a fraction of the sugar.
- **Tequila soda with fresh lime** (a simple "ranch water"). Choose 100% agave tequila; mixed tequilas (called "mixtos") contain other sugars and may have more additives.
- **Vodka or tequila with fresh grapefruit and soda.** A lighter take on a Paloma, if grapefruit is fine with your medications.
- **A tall glass, not a short one.** More mixer and ice per pour slows you down.
- **Ask for a standard pour.** Heavy-handed pours at home and some bars can make one drink closer to two.

And a few habits that matter more than any mixer:

1. **Eat a real meal before you start.** Food in your stomach slows alcohol absorption more than anything else you can do.
2. **Alternate every drink with a glass of water.** It slows your pace and gives you fluid.
3. **Keep to about one drink an hour.** That roughly matches what your liver can clear.
4. **Stick to one type of drink.** Mixing doesn't change the chemistry (the old "beer before liquor" rhyme isn't really true), but switching drinks often makes it harder to track how much you've had.
5. **Stop earlier than you think.** The last two drinks of the night tend to do the most damage to your morning.

## When a Hangover Means More Than a Hangover

Most hangovers, however miserable, get better with rest, fluids, and food within a day. A few situations are different and need medical help:

- **During or right after drinking:** confusion, vomiting that won't stop, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, very pale or bluish skin, low body temperature, or being hard to wake up. These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Call 911. Don't leave the person alone, and keep them on their side.
- **The next day:** symptoms that get worse rather than better after 24 hours, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, vomiting blood, or being unable to keep any fluids down.
- **If you mixed alcohol with medication** and feel unusually unwell, call your doctor or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US).

If you regularly feel shaky, anxious, or sweaty the morning after drinking and those feelings ease when you drink again, mention it to your doctor. That pattern is worth a conversation.

## Where Supplements Fit In

Mixers can make a night a bit gentler, but they can't change how your body processes the alcohol itself. Some people add a supplement to their routine for that reason.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data so far. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in everyone, and it does not make heavy drinking safe or lower your blood alcohol enough to drive. Some people find it helps them feel better the next morning when taken alongside sensible drinking habits. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when.

## The Bottom Line

The best mixer to avoid a hangover is soda water, and the best mixer of all is a glass of water between drinks. Pair it with a clear spirit like vodka, gin, or 100% agave tequila, and you've made the choice with the fewest downsides. Tonic and juice are fine in moderation but carry more sugar than they seem to. Diet mixers can raise your blood alcohol more than you'd expect, so treat them as slightly stronger drinks. Energy drinks are the one mixer worth skipping entirely.

None of these choices changes the basic rule: the amount you drink and how fast you drink it matter far more than what you mix it with.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the best mixer for vodka to avoid a hangover?**

Soda water (club soda or seltzer) with fresh lime is the best everyday choice. It has no sugar or caffeine and is easy to sip slowly. Still water is even simpler. Whatever you pick, drinking a glass of water between drinks and keeping to about one drink an hour matter more than the mixer.

**Is tonic water or soda water better for a hangover?**

Soda water is better. Regular tonic water contains a similar amount of sugar to regular soda, even though its bitter taste hides it. If you like the flavor of tonic, try half tonic and half soda water, or a light tonic.

**Do diet mixers make you drunker?**

They can. A 2013 study by Marczinski and Stamates found that vodka mixed with a diet soft drink produced higher breath alcohol readings than the same amount mixed with a regular one, without people feeling any more drunk. Sugar slows stomach emptying, so removing it lets alcohol absorb faster. If you use diet mixers, pace yourself and eat first.

**Does fruit juice help prevent a hangover?**

There is no good evidence that juice prevents hangovers or helps you sober up faster. It adds fluid and some nutrients, but it's high in sugar and makes alcohol easier to drink quickly. A splash of fresh juice in soda water is a good compromise.

**Are energy drinks a bad mixer for alcohol?**

Yes. Caffeine hides how drunk you feel without lowering your blood alcohol, which tends to lead people to drink more. The CDC links mixing alcohol with energy drinks to heavier drinking and riskier behavior. Energy drinks also disrupt sleep, which can make the next day worse.

**Does carbonation make a hangover worse?**

Carbonation may speed up how fast alcohol is absorbed for some people, which can raise your peak blood alcohol level. It doesn't directly cause a hangover. If fizzy drinks seem to hit you harder, use still water as a mixer or simply drink more slowly.

**Is coconut water a good mixer for alcohol?**

It's a decent one. It has less sugar than most juices and contains potassium. It won't fully make up for the extra urination alcohol causes, though, so it isn't a substitute for drinking water and pacing yourself.

**Which spirit and mixer combination gives the least hangover?**

A clear, low-congener spirit like vodka or gin with soda water is the combination with the fewest downsides. Darker spirits like whiskey, bourbon, and dark rum contain more congeners, which research links to worse hangovers in many people, whatever you mix them with.
